title: James P. Anderson's 1972 Report and the Origin of "Tiger Teams"
explainer: Before "red team" entered common use, the U.S. Air Force commissioned ad hoc "tiger teams" in the late 1960s to attack its own computer systems and see what broke - and every one of them succeeded. James P. Anderson's 1972 report to the Air Force, Computer Security Technology Planning Study, formalized this adversarial testing practice and introduced ideas like the "reference monitor" that still underlie how defenders reason about trusted versus untrusted code paths. Modern red-teaming inherits both the method and its original caveat: a system surviving an engagement proves the team didn't find a hole, not that no hole exists.
